Chapter 4: Embracing Self-Care and Personal Responsibility
As you start setting healthier boundaries and loosening your grip on control, there’s a new focus that begins to shine through—self-care.
And if you’re someone who’s always put others first, just the thought of looking after yourself might feel a bit strange—or even selfish.
But here’s the thing: self-care isn’t just a nice-to-have. It’s a must-have for your well-being, and for building truly healthy relationships.
When we talk about self-care, we mean showing yourself the same compassion and attention you so often give to everyone else.
It’s about tuning in to your physical, emotional, and even spiritual needs—realizing that your happiness and fulfillment matter, too.
Neglecting yourself doesn’t just leave you empty—it also affects the people around you, whether you notice it or not.
If you grew up in a codependent environment, you might have learned to downplay your own needs, or maybe even ignore them completely.
Does resting, picking up a hobby, or asking for help ever make you feel guilty? You’re not alone.
Over time, though, this kind of self-neglect just leads to exhaustion, resentment, and that hollow feeling inside.
So, how do you turn things around and truly nurture yourself?
Here are a few practical steps that can help:
Make time for things that bring you joy, help you unwind, or give you a sense of accomplishment—no matter how small.
Take care of your physical health, whether that means getting enough rest, eating well, or simply moving your body.
Let yourself feel and express your emotions—all of them. And try not to judge yourself for whatever comes up.
And don’t be afraid to reach out for support—from friends, a therapist, or maybe even a recovery group—when you need it.
But self-care is also about personal responsibility. That means taking ownership of your feelings and choices, instead of blaming others or your circumstances for how you feel.
It’s a big shift—from seeing yourself as a victim, to realizing you have the power to make changes from the inside out.
Remember, personal responsibility isn’t about taking on everyone else’s problems. It’s about asking yourself, “What do I need right now?” and “How can I meet that need?”
When you make this shift, it’s empowering—and suddenly, new possibilities for growth and fulfillment start to open up.
Think about the oxygen mask on an airplane. You’re always told to put on your own mask first before helping anyone else. That’s the perfect metaphor for self-care: it isn’t selfish, it’s absolutely essential if you want to be there for others.
Embracing self-care and personal responsibility also means letting go of that harsh inner critic and those impossible standards you might set for yourself.
So many people caught in codependent patterns believe that any mistake equals failure. But recovery is about learning self-compassion—treating yourself with the same kindness you’d offer a good friend.
And of course, this is a journey. There’ll be setbacks and moments of doubt, and that’s okay.
But every step you take toward self-care builds your resilience and confidence.
Over time, your focus shifts away from managing everyone else to truly nurturing yourself. And that’s what creates the foundation for healthier, more balanced relationships—with others, and with yourself.
